page5_img_1.png.title: WhoDo deployment pipeline: data sources to reviewer scores
page5_img_1.png.description: Diagram of the WhoDo recommendation pipeline showing inputs, storage, scoring, and outputs. Source Control Data, Review Data, and Deployment & Machine Data feed into a central SQL Database (annotated “analysis every four hours” to indicate periodic updates). A Pull Request invokes the WhoDo Scoring Model which queries the SQL Database and produces ranked reviewer suggestions (example outputs shown as Reviewer1 Score: 2.3, Reviewer2 Score: 4.5, Reviewer3 Score: 1.2). The figure illustrates the end-to-end flow from repository data to numeric reviewer scores used to recommend reviewers.

page4_img_fig2.png.title: Reviewer suggestion frequencies with and without load balancing
page4_img_fig2.png.description: A ranked bar chart comparing how often WhoDo suggested each reviewer when run without load balancing (blue bars) versus with aggressive load balancing (orange bars). The x‑axis lists reviewers sorted by decreasing suggestion frequency for the no-load‑balancing run (leftmost reviewers are the most frequently suggested), and the y‑axis is the number of suggestions (up to ~45). Without load balancing the distribution is highly skewed with a few reviewers suggested very frequently (peaks ~40+), while aggressive load balancing lowers those peaks and produces a much flatter distribution — several mid and low-ranked reviewers receive more suggestions (orange bars exceed blue) as load is redistributed. In the simulation (θ=0.5) the mean suggestion frequency drops slightly from 10.10 to 9.34 and the standard deviation falls from 10.17 to 5.67, indicating reduced imbalance at the cost of shifting suggestions toward less-frequent reviewers.

page7_img_1.png.title: Email responses: reasons for manually adding reviewers
page7_img_1.png.description: Stacked horizontal bars show counts of email replies (total N=28) grouped by repository, with three coded reasons in the legend: NotRelevant (blue diagonal), DifferentTeam (yellow), and Promptness (red dotted). The chart illustrates that many responses cite Promptness — for example one bar shows 7 promptness, 2 different-team and 1 not-relevant — and another bar shows 5 promptness-only responses. The paper explains this split: smaller repositories largely reported adding reviewers because they were available quickly (promptness), whereas responses from the large repository more often complained that suggested reviewers were from different teams or not relevant.

page9_img_1.png.title: Retrospective evaluation: PR hits, precision, recall, F1 by repository
page9_img_1.png.description: A table reporting WhoDo’s retrospective recommendation metrics for five repositories. For each repo it lists total pull-requests, PR Hits (P@1) as count and percent (e.g., SmallRepo1: 170/190 = 89.47%; MediumRepo: 199/289 = 68.85%; SmallRepo3: 254/263 = 96.57%; LargeRepo: 191/234 = 81.62%), total suggestions and total reviewers considered, and the number of useful suggestions (for example SmallRepo1: 560 suggestions with 266 useful). The rightmost columns show precision, recall and F1 (reported as decimals) which vary by repo — SmallRepo3 has the best F1 (0.57) and MediumRepo the lowest (0.34) — indicating WhoDo frequently included at least one correct reviewer (high P@1) but precision/recall of the full recommended lists were mixed across projects. Overall the table shows strong PR-hit rates (≈69–97%) while precision and recall remain moderate, reflecting that top-1 suggestions are often useful even when the full 3-item recommendation list does not fully match all actual reviewers.

page4_img_fig1.png.title: Reviewer load vs active open reviews for linear and exponential θ values
page4_img_fig1.png.description: Line chart showing Load(reviewer) on the y-axis versus Active Open Reviews (1–8) on the x-axis, comparing four curves: a linear baseline (blue) and exponential penalties e^{0.2x} (orange), e^{0.4x} (gray), and e^{0.5x} (yellow). The plot illustrates how the exponential load function e^{θ·TotalOpenReviews} steepens as θ increases: for example, at 4 active reviews e^{0.5·4} ≈ 7.4 while e^{0.2·4} ≈ 2.2 and the linear baseline ≈ 4; by 8 active reviews e^{0.5·8} ≈ 54.6, e^{0.4·8} ≈ 24.5, e^{0.2·8} ≈ 5.0, and the linear ≈ 8. The figure is used in the paper to show that larger θ values produce much more aggressive load penalties (i.e., stronger down-weighting of reviewers with many open reviews), giving deployers an intuition for selecting θ.
